items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: He taught me a great deal of the bebop vocabulary... Every drummer that went through that band had that famous 22 Chinese cymbal... he would ask you to play that.

ctx.x: Was jazz in particular sort of banned by the Castro regime? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

Sometimes. Most of the time anything coming from the Western countries, like the Beatles, Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Dizzy Gillespie. That was the music of the enemy and the ideology back then was that the enemy was trying to penetrate our ideology any way possible. So music was one of the ways to penetrate our socialist ideology. So yes it was prohibited many times, it was prohibited to play music, you got in trouble for listening to the music. The only times we were able to play, once in a blue moon was when…
Can you remember specifically what it was about the Nat King Cole LP that grabbed your attention?

items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Dizzy Gillespie needs a drummer for tonight... I was sitting behind Dizzy Gillespie on drums playing at a club in Manhattan... Dizzy, my dear friend, my father, my brother... he did just not talk to me about what he wanted me to play in his band

ctx.x: That’s a terrific point and observation. I wanted to ask you when you actually were on the boat coming from Cuba to Florida, can you go back and remember your state of mind? What were you thinking, what were you hoping for?

Well first of all I was looking for freedom. In my case in particular my life in Cuba was unbearable. I never liked the system, just because the reason that I was not, I disagreed with the system that was against four guys from Liverpool with long hair and tight pants, three guitars and a drum. I didn’t know the message that they were conveying at that time because my English when I arrived into the United States, my English was zero. I had no club about English language. So I don’t know that what they were…

leave the island. Because I knew my future wasn’t in the country where I would not be allowed to express myself musically speaking. Let’s put politics aside, musically speaking. So I always, my dream was always coming to the United States because the music that I wanted to play and my heroes were here. I think that in our previous interview I said that my ultimate dream when I was in Cuba after I became a musician and I knew that jazz was the music that I wanted to play, my ultimate dreams was watching my heroes…
